fuentes/epitome-de-la-conquista-del-nuev.texto: Epitome of the Conquest of the New Kingdom of Granada
Anonymous (attributed to Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada)

Brief anonymous account of the expedition of Jiménez de Quesada from Santa Marta and of the Muisca country: its two great lords (the Bogotá and the Tunja), its towns, its markets for salt, mantas and gold, its shrines and its wars with the Panches. The manuscript is kept in the Archivo Histórico Nacional in Madrid and was published by Marcos Jiménez de la Espada in 1889. It is attributed to Quesada or to someone in his circle; the date and the authorship are debated.
It is the earliest description of Muisca society, written by someone in or close to the expedition, before the great chronicles of the 17th century.

fuentes/indianische-historia/resumen.texto: Account of Federmann's first expedition (1530–1531) from Coro southward, printed in Hagenau in 1557, years after his death. It describes the Caquetío, Jirajara, Ayamán and other peoples, their wars and alliances, the use of interpreters and the capture of Indigenous people by the expedition.

fuentes/indianische-historia/por_que_imp.texto: It is the first printed book devoted to present-day Venezuela and one of the few written sources by the German conquistadors of the Welser.

fuentes/indianische-historia/leer.0.titu.texto: Original Hagenau edition (1557) at Internet Archive

fuentes/capitulacion-de-los-welser/titul.texto: Royal Capitulation with the Welser Agents for the Governorship of Venezuela

fuentes/capitulacion-de-los-welser/resum.texto: Agreement signed in Madrid on March 27, 1528 with Heinrich Ehinger and Hieronymus Sailer, agents of the Welser house of Augsburg, to conquer and settle the coast between Cabo de la Vela and Maracapana, with the obligation to found towns and fortresses and to bring German colonists and miners. That same year the agents obtained a license to introduce 4,000 African slaves into the Indies.

fuentes/capitulacion-de-los-welser/por_q.texto: It is the legal basis of the only governorship in Spanish America granted to a foreign commercial house.

fuentes/elegias-de-varones-ilustres/titu.texto: Elegies of Illustrious Men of the Indies

fuentes/elegias-de-varones-ilustres/resu.texto: Verse chronicle of more than a hundred thousand hendecasyllables on the discovery and conquest of the Antilles, Venezuela, Cartagena, Santa Marta, Popayán and the New Kingdom of Granada. Only the first part was printed during the author's lifetime (Madrid, 1589); the rest appeared in the 19th century, and the fourth part, the Historia del Nuevo Reino de Granada, in 1886–1887. Castellanos uses testimony from conquistadors he knew and describes Indigenous wars, customs and rites.

fuentes/elegias-de-varones-ilustres/por_.texto: It is the earliest and most extensive source for many episodes of the conquest of Colombia and Venezuela. It mixes firsthand testimony, rumor and epic rhetoric, and its value varies from episode to episode.

fuentes/elegias-de-varones-ilustres/leer.texto: Fourth part (Historia del Nuevo Reino de Granada), volume 1 of the 1886 edition, at Internet Archive

fuentes/recopilacion-historial-aguado/re.texto: Chronicle in two parts on the conquest of Santa Marta and the New Kingdom of Granada and on Venezuela, including the expedition of Ursúa and Aguirre, written with testimony from conquistadors. Aguado took it to Spain around 1575 to have it printed; it went through the censorship of the Council of the Indies and remained unpublished until the early 20th century.

fuentes/recopilacion-historial-aguado/po.texto: It is the earliest prose chronicle of the New Kingdom; Pedro Simón used it and copied it extensively.

fuentes/relacion-de-francisco-vazquez/ti.texto: Account of Everything That Happened on the Expedition to Omagua and El Dorado

fuentes/relacion-de-francisco-vazquez/re.texto: Account by a soldier of Pedro de Ursúa's expedition who, after following Lope de Aguirre down the Amazon and as far as Margarita, defected to the loyalists. It narrates the departure from Peru, the murder of Ursúa, the proclamation of Fernando de Guzmán as “prince,” the massacres ordered by Aguirre and his end in Barquisimeto, and it includes a copy of Aguirre's letter to the king. It circulated in copies, one of them signed by Pedrarias de Almesto.

fuentes/relacion-de-francisco-vazquez/po.texto: It is the most detailed and closest account of the expedition. Like all those written by survivors, it was written to show that its author had not been an accomplice of the rebel.

fuentes/carta-de-lope-de-aguirre/titulo.texto: Letter from Lope de Aguirre to Philip II

fuentes/carta-de-lope-de-aguirre/resumen.texto: Letter in which Aguirre declares himself in rebellion and renounces being a vassal of the king, whom he accuses of ingratitude toward the conquistadors of Peru. He denounces the corruption of judges (oidores), governors and friars, recounts in his own way the murder of Ursúa and the descent of the Amazon, and defies the Crown. It is known through copies included in the accounts of the expedition.

fuentes/carta-de-lope-de-aguirre/por_que.texto: It is an exceptional document of a conquistador's break with the Crown. In the 19th and 20th centuries it was read as the first declaration of American independence, a reading that historians consider anachronistic.

fuentes/gramatica-muisca-lugo/titulo.texto: Grammar of the General Language of the New Kingdom, Called Mosca

fuentes/gramatica-muisca-lugo/resumen.texto: Grammar of Muisca printed in Madrid in 1619, with a confessional and texts for doctrine. The language had a chair in Santafé from the late 16th century, and doctrinal priests had to pass an examination to practice.

fuentes/gramatica-muisca-lugo/por_que_im.texto: It is the main source on a Chibchan language that ceased to be spoken in the 18th century. It also shows the policy of evangelizing in Indigenous languages that Charles III abandoned in 1770 when he ordered Castilianization.

fuentes/gramatica-muisca-lugo/leer.0.tit.texto: Original Madrid edition (1619) at Internet Archive

fuentes/de-instauranda-aethiopum-salute/.texto: De instauranda Aethiopum salute (The Nature, Sacred and Secular Order of All Ethiopians)

Treatise printed in Seville in 1627 and reissued, expanded and with a Latin title, in Madrid in 1647. It describes the kingdoms, peoples and languages of Africa from which the enslaved people arriving at Cartagena came, the crossing on the ships, the sale and the mistreatment, and it proposes a method to baptize and catechize them with interpreters. Sandoval sets out the doubts of theologians about the justice of the slave trade and criticizes the cruelty of masters, but he does not call for abolition.
It is the first extensive work written in the Americas about enslaved Africans and an early ethnographic source on West and Central Africa.

fuentes/noticias-historiales-simon/titul.texto: Historical News of the Conquests of Tierra Firme in the Western Indies

fuentes/noticias-historiales-simon/resum.texto: Chronicle in three parts. The first, printed in Cuenca in 1627, deals with Venezuela and the expedition of Ursúa and Aguirre; the second and third, on the New Kingdom, Cartagena and Santa Marta, remained unpublished until 1882–1892. Simón used Aguado, Castellanos and witnesses, and describes Muisca religion: shrines, idols, offerings in lagoons, the sacrifice of the moxas, and the wars between the zipas and zaques.

fuentes/noticias-historiales-simon/por_q.texto: It is the basis of almost everything written afterward about the Muiscas. Several of its reports, such as the chronology of the zipas, have no other independent source.

fuentes/noticias-historiales-simon/leer..texto: First part, Cuenca edition (1627), at Internet Archive

fuentes/el-carnero/titulo.texto: El Carnero (Conquest and Discovery of the New Kingdom of Granada)

fuentes/el-carnero/resumen.texto: Chronicle of Santafé from the conquest to 1638, with many stories of crimes, love affairs and lawsuits among the colonial elite. It includes a description of the ceremony in which the heir of the Guatavita chiefdom, covered in gold dust, entered a raft on the lagoon and threw offerings, as the author says he heard from a cacique friend. It circulated in manuscript and was printed in 1859.

fuentes/el-carnero/por_que_importa.texto: It is the classic source for the ceremony that gave rise to the legend of El Dorado. It was written a century after the conquest and relies on secondhand information.

fuentes/historia-general-piedrahita/titu.texto: General History of the Conquests of the New Kingdom of Granada

fuentes/historia-general-piedrahita/resu.texto: History of the Muiscas and of the conquest of the New Kingdom until the mid-16th century, printed in Antwerp in 1688. Piedrahita reorganized Castellanos and Simón and used the lost Compendio historial of Jiménez de Quesada. He gives the chronology of the zipas and zaques, the laws attributed to Nemequene and the description of rites that later authors repeated.

fuentes/historia-general-piedrahita/por_.texto: It established the classic image of a Muisca monarchy comparable to that of the Incas, an image that current archaeology qualifies.

fuentes/historia-de-las-misiones-de-los-.texto: History of the Missions of the Llanos of Casanare and the Orinoco and Meta Rivers

Chronicle of the Jesuit missions of the Llanos and the Orinoco, written by the Jesuit Juan Rivero and published in Bogotá in 1883. It recounts the founding of the reductions of the Achagua, Sáliva, Betoy and other peoples, the epidemics, and the wars with the Caribs, who attacked the missions and sold captives.
It is the main history of the Llanos missions before Gumilla, written from within the order.

fuentes/historia-de-venezuela-oviedo-y-b.texto: History of the Conquest and Settlement of the Province of Venezuela

First part, the only one published, of a history of Venezuela from the first voyages to the late 16th century, printed in Madrid in 1723. It recounts the Welser expeditions, the founding of the towns, the conquest of the Caracas valley and the war with Guaicaipuro and other caciques, with documents from the Caracas cabildo.
It is the source for almost everything repeated about Guaicaipuro and the conquest of central Venezuela, written a century and a half after the events.

fuentes/el-orinoco-ilustrado/resumen.texto: Natural, civil and geographic history of the Orinoco basin and its Jesuit missions, printed in Madrid in 1741 and expanded in 1745. It describes the Achagua, Sáliva, Otomaco, Caribs and other peoples, their wars, the sale of Carib captives to the Dutch of the Essequibo, curare, the geophagy of the Otomacos and the infanticide of girls that he attributes to some mothers. It defends the missions against Carib attacks.

fuentes/el-orinoco-ilustrado/por_que_imp.texto: It is the reference work on the Orinoco in the 18th century. It combines direct observation with the view of a missionary who justified the war against the Caribs.

fuentes/el-orinoco-ilustrado/leer.0.titu.texto: Volume 1 of the Madrid edition (1745), from the Wellcome Library, at Internet Archive

fuentes/el-orinoco-ilustrado/leer.1.titu.texto: Volume 2 of the Madrid edition (1745), from the Wellcome Library, at Internet Archive

fuentes/saggio-di-storia-americana/titul.texto: Essay on American History (Saggio di storia americana)

fuentes/saggio-di-storia-americana/resum.texto: Four-volume work printed in Rome by an expelled Jesuit. It describes the middle Orinoco and the life of the Tamanaco, Maipure and other peoples of its missions. The third volume compares languages and groups several of them into families, among them Carib and the one now called Arawakan.

fuentes/saggio-di-storia-americana/por_q.texto: It is one of the foundations of South American comparative linguistics and a detailed ethnography of the Orinoco reductions before the expulsion of 1767.

fuentes/saggio-di-storia-americana/leer..texto: One volume of the Rome edition at Internet Archive

fuentes/discoverie-of-guiana/resumen.texto: Account of the 1595 expedition to Trinidad and the lower Orinoco, with the capture of San José de Oruña and the seizure of Antonio de Berrío. Raleigh describes the river peoples and their hostility toward the Spaniards, repeats reports of the golden city of Manoa and of men without heads, and proposes that Elizabeth I conquer Guiana.

fuentes/discoverie-of-guiana/por_que_imp.texto: It spread the legend of El Dorado in Europe and was an argument for English colonization. Its exaggerations were criticized already in its own time.

fuentes/discoverie-of-guiana/leer.0.titu.texto: Original London edition (1596) at Internet Archive

fuentes/narrative-of-surinam-stedman/tit.texto: Narrative of a Five Years' Expedition Against the Revolted Negroes of Surinam

fuentes/narrative-of-surinam-stedman/res.texto: Memoirs of the campaigns against the Boni maroons in which the author served, with descriptions of nature, of life on the plantations and of the punishments of enslaved people, illustrated with engravings, several of them by William Blake. The editor softened the manuscript; Richard and Sally Price published the complete original text in 1988.

fuentes/narrative-of-surinam-stedman/por.texto: It was read as testimony against slavery, although its author was not an abolitionist. It is one of the main sources on Surinam in the 18th century.

fuentes/narrative-of-surinam-stedman/lee.texto: Volume 1 of the London edition (1796) at Internet Archive

fuentes/tratado-de-breda-1667/autor.texto: England, United Provinces, France and Denmark

fuentes/tratado-de-breda-1667/resumen.texto: Peace treaties signed on July 31, 1667, which ended the Second Anglo-Dutch War. Each party kept what it held: England kept New Amsterdam (New York), and the United Provinces kept Surinam, which Abraham Crijnssen's Zeeland fleet had taken from the English that year.

fuentes/tratado-de-breda-1667/por_que_im.texto: It fixed the Dutch presence in Surinam for a century and a half. Presenting it as an “exchange” of New York for Surinam is a simplification.

fuentes/tratados-con-los-cimarrones-de-s.texto: Peace Treaties with the Ndyuka (1760) and the Saramaka (1762)
Government of the Colony of Surinam

Treaties of the Surinam government with the Ndyuka maroons (October 10, 1760) and the Saramaka (September 19, 1762), completed with that of the Matawai (1767), after decades of war. They recognized their freedom and territory, gave them periodic gifts of weapons, tools and cloth, and obliged them to return new runaways and not to approach the plantations without permission.

Together with the Jamaican treaties of 1739, they are among the first recognitions of free maroon peoples by a colonial government. The Saramaka and Ndyuka keep them in their oral memory as the basis of their freedom.

fuentes/capitulaciones-de-zipaquira/auto.texto: Comunero leaders and commissioners of the Audiencia of Santafé

fuentes/capitulaciones-de-zipaquira/resu.texto: Agreement of 35 chapters signed on June 8, 1781, between the comunero leaders and the commissioners of the Audiencia, with the mediation of Archbishop Caballero y Góngora. It suppressed or lowered the new taxes and monopolies, removed the regent visitor Gutiérrez de Piñeres, asked for preference for those born in America in offices, and granted Indigenous people a reduction of tribute and of resguardo lands. Viceroy Flórez disowned it, and the authorities declared it null.

fuentes/capitulaciones-de-zipaquira/por_.texto: It is the written program of the largest rebellion of the New Kingdom in the 18th century. Its annulment and the punishment of Galán marked the political memory of New Granada.

fuentes/flora-de-la-expedicion-botanica/.texto: Flora of the Royal Botanical Expedition of the New Kingdom of Granada

Collection of more than six thousand plates of plants painted by the draftsmen of the Botanical Expedition, many of them Creoles, mestizos and people from Quito trained in the workshop at Mariquita and Santafé, such as Salvador Rizo, with descriptions and an herbarium. In 1816 Morillo sent it to Madrid, where it is kept at the Royal Botanical Garden; it has been published since 1954 in a joint edition of Spain and Colombia.
It is the largest work of botanical iconography of the Enlightenment in the Americas and the main fruit of a scientific enterprise of the Crown directed from Santafé.

fuentes/papel-periodico-de-santafe/titul.texto: Papel Periódico de la Ciudad de Santafé de Bogotá

fuentes/papel-periodico-de-santafe/resum.texto: Weekly founded in 1791 by the Cuban librarian Manuel del Socorro Rodríguez with the support of Viceroy Ezpeleta. It published news, articles on science, economics and morals, and texts by the city's Enlightenment thinkers until 1797.

fuentes/papel-periodico-de-santafe/por_q.texto: It was the first regular newspaper of the New Kingdom of Granada.

fuentes/derechos-del-hombre-narino/titul.texto: Rights of Man (translation by Antonio Nariño)

fuentes/derechos-del-hombre-narino/resum.texto: Spanish translation of the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, taken from a French book about the National Constituent Assembly, which Nariño printed at his Patriotic Press in Santafé at the end of 1793. He distributed few copies and destroyed the rest when he learned that he was under investigation. He was tried and in 1795 sentenced to ten years in a presidio in Africa and the confiscation of his property.

fuentes/derechos-del-hombre-narino/por_q.texto: The trial turned him into the “precursor” of New Granadan independence, and it shows the control of the ideas of the French Revolution in Spanish America.

fuentes/viaje-a-las-regiones-equinoccial.texto: Voyage to the Equinoctial Regions of the New Continent

Account of the journey of Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland through Venezuela, the Orinoco and the Casiquiare, Cuba and New Granada, published in Paris in three volumes between 1814 and 1825 and left unfinished. It describes nature, the Capuchin and Franciscan missions, Indigenous peoples and slavery in Caracas and Cuba, and it confirms that the Casiquiare links the Orinoco and Amazon basins.
It is one of the central works of 19th-century science. It fixed the European image of tropical America on the eve of independence.
Volume 1 of the 1826 Spanish translation at Internet Archive

fuentes/memorial-de-agravios/titulo.texto: Memorial of Grievances (Representation of the Cabildo of Santafé to the Central Junta)

fuentes/memorial-de-agravios/resumen.texto: Representation written by Camilo Torres in November 1809 for the cabildo of Santafé, which protested that the Central Junta of Spain gave all of America nine deputies, against thirty-six from the Peninsula. It demands equal rights between Spanish Americans and Europeans and warns of the risk of separation. The cabildo did not send it, and it was published only in 1832.

fuentes/memorial-de-agravios/por_que_imp.texto: It is the most cited text of pre-1810 Creole autonomism in New Granada.

fuentes/acta-del-19-de-abril-de-1810/res.texto: Act of the Caracas cabildo which, after forcing the resignation of Captain General Vicente Emparan, assumed government in the name of Ferdinand VII and disavowed the authority of the Council of Regency of Spain. It gave rise to the Supreme Junta of Caracas, which abolished the Indigenous tribute, banned the slave trade and called a congress of the provinces.

fuentes/acta-del-19-de-abril-de-1810/por.texto: It is the start of the process that led to the declaration of independence of 1811.

fuentes/acta-del-20-de-julio-de-1810/tit.texto: Act of the Junta of Santafé of July 20, 1810

fuentes/acta-del-20-de-julio-de-1810/res.texto: Act signed on the night of July 20, 1810, by the open cabildo of Santafé, which created a Supreme Junta of the New Kingdom presided at first by Viceroy Antonio Amar y Borbón. The junta recognized Ferdinand VII on the condition that he come to reign in America, and it announced a federative constitution for the provinces.

fuentes/acta-del-20-de-julio-de-1810/por.texto: Colombia celebrates it as its act of independence, although the formal break with the Crown came later and province by province (Cartagena in 1811, Cundinamarca in 1813).

fuentes/acta-de-independencia-de-venezue.texto: Act of the Declaration of Independence of Venezuela

Act approved on July 5, 1811, by the congress of seven provinces of the Captaincy General (Maracaibo, Coro and Guayana remained loyal to the Regency). It declares the United Provinces of Venezuela free and independent states, independent of the Spanish Crown, with arguments from natural law, the grievances of three centuries of Spanish rule and the crisis of the monarchy of 1808–1810.
It is the first formal declaration of independence of a territory in Spanish America.

fuentes/constitucion-de-venezuela-de-181.texto: Federal Constitution for the States of Venezuela

Constitution enacted on December 21, 1811. It established a federal republic with a three-person executive and the Catholic religion as the only religion. It declared the legal equality of pardos and Indigenous people, whom it released from the regime of tribute and guardianship, and it prohibited the slave trade without abolishing slavery.

It is often called the first constitution in Spanish America, although that of the state of Cundinamarca, monarchical and provincial, dates from April 1811. It remained in force until the fall of the First Republic in 1812, and Bolívar blamed its federalism for the defeat.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-cartagena/resumen.texto: Memorandum of December 15, 1812, addressed to the citizens of New Granada. Bolívar attributes the fall of the First Republic of Venezuela to federalism, to indulgence toward enemies, to the lack of a regular army and to the use the clergy made of the earthquake of 1812. He asks for help to recover Caracas.

fuentes/manifiesto-de-cartagena/por_que_.texto: It is his first major political text and the program of the Admirable Campaign of 1813.

fuentes/decreto-de-guerra-a-muerte/titul.texto: Decree of War to the Death

fuentes/decreto-de-guerra-a-muerte/resum.texto: Proclamation signed in Trujillo on June 15, 1813, during the Admirable Campaign. It announces that Spaniards and Canary Islanders who did not actively cooperate with the patriot cause would be killed even if indifferent, and that Americans would be pardoned even if guilty. It responded to the executions of patriots by royalist leaders such as Monteverde, Zuazola and Antoñanzas.

fuentes/decreto-de-guerra-a-muerte/por_q.texto: It authorized the execution of prisoners and civilians on account of their origin, and it was in effect until the 1820 treaty regularizing the war. Its defenders present it as a reprisal that forced people to take sides. Its critics see it as a policy of executions by nationality that worsened the violence.

fuentes/discurso-de-angostura/resumen.texto: Address with which Bolívar opened the Congress of Angostura on February 15, 1819. He presents a draft constitution with a strong executive, a hereditary senate and a “moral power.” He asks the congress to confirm the freedom of the enslaved and proposes uniting Venezuela and New Granada.

fuentes/discurso-de-angostura/por_que_im.texto: It is the most complete exposition of his constitutional thought, which combines the British model with institutions taken from antiquity.

fuentes/ley-fundamental-de-1819/titulo.texto: Fundamental Law of the Republic of Colombia

fuentes/ley-fundamental-de-1819/resumen.texto: Law of December 17, 1819, which united Venezuela and New Granada in the Republic of Colombia, divided into three departments (Venezuela, Cundinamarca and Quito, the last still in royalist hands), with a president and a vice president. It called a general congress in Cúcuta for 1821.

fuentes/ley-fundamental-de-1819/por_que_.texto: It is the birth certificate of Gran Colombia.

fuentes/ley-de-manumision-de-1821/titulo.texto: Law on the Freedom of Births, Manumission, and Abolition of the Slave Trade

fuentes/ley-de-manumision-de-1821/resume.texto: Law of July 1821 that declared free the children of enslaved women born after its publication, with the obligation to work for their mother's master until age 18. It created manumission boards funded by a tax on inheritances and prohibited the slave trade. Slavery was fully abolished in New Granada in 1851 and in Venezuela in 1854.

fuentes/ley-de-manumision-de-1821/por_qu.texto: It was the first free-womb law of Gran Colombia. The boards freed few enslaved people, and abolition took thirty years.

fuentes/constitucion-de-cucuta/titulo.texto: Constitution of the Republic of Colombia (Cúcuta Constitution)

fuentes/constitucion-de-cucuta/resumen.texto: Constitution enacted on August 30, 1821, in the Villa del Rosario de Cúcuta. It organized a central republic with a president serving four years, a two-chamber congress and indirect elections with property requirements. The congress elected Bolívar president and Santander vice president.

fuentes/constitucion-de-cucuta/por_que_i.texto: It organized Gran Colombia until its dissolution in 1830. The same congress abolished the Indigenous tribute and ordered that the resguardos be distributed as individual property, a measure that made their loss easier.

fuentes/semanario-del-nuevo-reino-de-gra.texto: Semanario del Nuevo Reino de Granada

Scientific periodical that Caldas published in Santafé between 1808 and 1810, with his “State of the Geography of the Viceroyalty,” studies in astronomy, botany, meteorology and economics, and articles by other enlightened Creoles. In “On the Influence of Climate on Organized Beings,” Caldas argued that climate shapes the bodies and character of peoples, an idea of the time that is now rejected.
It shows the scientific program and the territorial vision of the Creole elite on the eve of independence.
1808 issues (original Santafé edition), John Carter Brown Library, at Internet Archive

fuentes/monumentale-vorgeschichtliche-ku.texto: Monumental Prehistoric Art: Excavations at the Magdalena Sources in Colombia

Report on Preuss’s excavations at San Agustín in 1913-1914, with the recording and photography of the statues, tombs and mounds and an interpretation of their iconography by comparison with Indigenous myths. Preuss took several statues to Berlin, which led to Colombian complaints.
It was the first scientific description of the San Agustín statuary and the basis for later studies.

fuentes/colombia-reichel-dolmatoff/resum.texto: Synthesis of Colombian archaeology from the earliest hunters to the chiefdoms the Spanish encountered, including the author’s excavations on the Caribbean coast, among them the early pottery of Puerto Hormiga. It proposes a developmental sequence that organized the field for decades.

fuentes/colombia-reichel-dolmatoff/por_q.texto: It was the first scientific overview of Colombia’s prehistory and is still cited, although many of its dates and schemes have been revised.

fuentes/historia-economica-colmenares/ti.texto: Economic and Social History of Colombia, 1537-1719

fuentes/historia-economica-colmenares/re.texto: Study of the economy and society of the New Kingdom in its first two centuries: the encomienda, tribute and personal services, the decline of the Indigenous population according to inspection tours (visitas) and tribute assessments (tasaciones), gold mining with Indigenous and then African labor, and the formation of the hacienda. Colmenares worked with series of archival documents rather than with chronicles.

fuentes/historia-economica-colmenares/po.texto: It renewed Colombian historiography and remains the reference on forced labor and Indigenous demography in the New Kingdom.

fuentes/the-people-and-the-king/titulo.texto: The People and the King: The Comunero Revolution in Colombia, 1781

fuentes/the-people-and-the-king/resumen.texto: Posthumous study of the Comunero revolt, its fiscal causes and the Capitulations of Zipaquirá. Phelan argues that the comuneros defended an “unwritten constitution” of negotiation between the kingdom and the Crown that the Bourbon reforms had broken, not a project of independence.

fuentes/the-people-and-the-king/por_que_.texto: It displaced the nationalist reading that saw the comuneros as precursors of 1810. His thesis is very influential today, although other authors stress more the social and Indigenous component of the revolt.

fuentes/lords-of-the-tiger-spirit/titulo.texto: Lords of the Tiger Spirit: A History of the Caribs in Colonial Venezuela and Guyana, 1498-1820

fuentes/lords-of-the-tiger-spirit/resume.texto: History of the Kari’ña Carib peoples of the Orinoco and the Guianas based on Spanish, Dutch and English documents. It shows how the Caribs used their alliances with the Dutch of the Essequibo to obtain weapons and tools in exchange for captives from other peoples, and how the label “Carib” served the Spanish to justify the enslavement of those who received it.

fuentes/lords-of-the-tiger-spirit/por_qu.texto: It is the standard reference on the Caribs of the continent and on the political use of the accusation of cannibalism.

fuentes/first-time-price/titulo.texto: First-Time: The Historical Vision of an Afro-American People

fuentes/first-time-price/resumen.texto: History of the Saramaka of Suriname in their founding era, up to the 1762 peace treaty, written by combining oral tradition, which the Saramaka themselves consider restricted, with documents from the Dutch archives.

fuentes/first-time-price/por_que_importa.texto: It is a classic work on maroons and on how to bring oral memory and the colonial archive together.

fuentes/colombia-before-independence/tit.texto: Colombia before Independence: Economy, Society and Politics under Bourbon Rule

fuentes/colombia-before-independence/res.texto: Study of the Viceroyalty of New Granada in the 18th century: slave-based gold mining in the Pacific and Antioquia, trade and smuggling through the Caribbean, the Bourbon reforms and the Comunero revolt, and the crisis of 1808-1810.

fuentes/colombia-before-independence/por.texto: It is the standard synthesis on Bourbon New Granada in English.

fuentes/invading-colombia/titulo.texto: Invading Colombia: Spanish Accounts of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada’s Conquest Expedition

fuentes/invading-colombia/resumen.texto: Critical edition and annotated translation of the earliest documents on the conquest of Muisca territory: the Epítome, the account by Juan de San Martín and Antonio de Lebrija (1539), sworn testimonies (probanzas) and other statements by participants, with a study of how each one told the events according to his own interests.

fuentes/invading-colombia/por_que_import.texto: It brings together the early primary sources on the Muisca conquest, which later chronicles reworked.

fuentes/los-muiscas-langebaek/titulo.texto: The Muiscas: The Millennial History of a Chibcha People

fuentes/los-muiscas-langebaek/resumen.texto: Synthesis of Muisca history from its antecedents on the highlands to the conquest and the colonial period, based on regional archaeology and critical reading of the chronicles. Langebaek questions the image of a centralized Muisca state and of a “confederation,” and describes a society of chiefdoms with inequalities and conflicts.

fuentes/los-muiscas-langebaek/por_que_im.texto: It is the most recent synthesis on the Muiscas written by an archaeologist who excavated them.

fuentes/los-welser-friede/titulo.texto: The Welsers in the Conquest of Venezuela

fuentes/los-welser-friede/resumen.texto: Documentary study of the Welser governorship, based on the Archivo de Indias: the capitulations, the expeditions of Ehinger, Federmann, Hohermuth and Hutten, the capture and sale of Indigenous people as slaves, and the house’s lawsuits with the Crown.

fuentes/los-welser-friede/por_que_import.texto: It is the reference work on the Germans in the conquest of Venezuela, based on documents rather than on the chroniclers’ tradition.

personas/saguamanchica/resumen.texto: Zipa of Bacatá according to the chronology reconstructed by Pedro Simón and Piedrahita. He waged war against the Fusagasugá, the Panches and the zaque of Hunza, and died around 1490 in the battle of Chocontá, in which the zaque Michuá also fell.

personas/nemequene/resumen.texto: Zipa of Bacatá around 1490-1514 according to 17th-century chroniclers. Piedrahita attributes to him a very severe code of laws (“código de Nemequene”), known only from that late source, so its exact content is doubtful.

personas/tisquesusa/resumen.texto: Last independent zipa of Bacatá, the Muisca lordship of the south, whose name (“Bogotá” in the earliest sources) remained in the Spanish city. He avoided combat with Jiménez de Quesada’s force and died in 1537 in a night attack by the Spanish near Facatativá, at the hands of a soldier who did not recognize him, according to the chronicles.

personas/sagipa/resumen.texto: Successor of Tisquesusa, regarded as a usurper by the Muisca nobility. He allied with the Spanish against the Panches (Tocarema, 1538) and was then arrested and tortured to make him hand over his predecessor’s treasure; he died in prison in 1539. That death was one of the charges in the trial against Jiménez de Quesada.

personas/quemuenchatocha/resumen.texto: Zaque of Hunza (Tunja), the northern Muisca lordship, when the Spanish arrived. In August 1537 Jiménez de Quesada entered Hunza, took him prisoner and seized the gold from his enclosure; freed, he died shortly afterward in Ramiriquí.

personas/aquiminzaque/resumen.texto: Last zaque of Hunza, subjected to the Spanish. In 1540 Hernán Pérez de Quesada had him beheaded in Tunja along with other caciques, accused of plotting an uprising; the accusation is known from Spanish chronicles.

personas/alonso-de-ojeda/resumen.texto: Native of Cuenca who accompanied Columbus on his second voyage. In 1499 he explored the coast of present-day Venezuela with Juan de la Cosa and Amerigo Vespucci; in 1502 he founded a short-lived settlement on the Guajira and in 1510 the fort of San Sebastián de Urabá, which was lost that same year. He died poor in Santo Domingo.

personas/rodrigo-de-bastidas/resumen.texto: Scribe from Triana who in 1501, with Juan de la Cosa, explored the Caribbean coast of Colombia from Cabo de la Vela to Darién. He founded Santa Marta in 1525; his own men stabbed him in 1526, partly because he forbade them to plunder peaceful Indigenous peoples, and he died in Cuba.

personas/pedro-de-heredia/resumen.texto: Native of Madrid who founded Cartagena de Indias in 1533 and looted the gold tombs of the Zenú in the Sinú (1534). His residency trials charged him with mistreating Indigenous people and appropriating Crown gold; he died in a shipwreck on his return to Spain in 1554.

personas/gonzalo-jimenez-de-quesada/resu.texto: Lawyer born in Granada or Córdoba (the sources disagree) who led from Santa Marta (1536) the expedition that conquered Muisca territory and founded Santafé de Bogotá (1538). He was tried in Spain for the death of Sagipa and other charges, returned to the New Kingdom as marshal, wrote works that are mostly lost today, and in 1569-1572 searched for El Dorado in the Llanos without success.

personas/hernan-perez-de-quesada/resumen.texto: Brother of Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, he governed the New Kingdom after the latter’s departure (1539). He ordered the execution of the zaque Aquiminzaque (1540) and in 1541-1542 led a costly expedition in search of El Dorado; he died struck by lightning in 1544, according to the chronicles.

personas/ambrosius-ehinger/resumen.texto: Merchant from Ulm, the first governor of Venezuela for the Welsers (1529). He founded Maracaibo and led expeditions toward the lake and the Magdalena in which he captured and sold Indigenous people as slaves; he died in 1533 from a poisoned arrow.

personas/nikolaus-federmann/resumen.texto: Welser agent born in Ulm. He recounted his first expedition (1530-1531) in the Indianische Historia; on the second (1536-1539) he crossed the Llanos and the Andes and reached the Bogotá savanna in 1539, where he met Jiménez de Quesada and Belalcázar. He died in Spain, embroiled in lawsuits with the Welsers.

personas/philipp-von-hutten/resumen.texto: Franconian nobleman who took part in Georg Hohermuth’s expedition (1535-1538) and led another in search of El Dorado (1541-1546). On his return, in 1546, the Spanish governor Juan de Carvajal had him beheaded together with Bartolomé Welser the Younger; his letters are a source on the German expeditions.

personas/pedro-de-ursua/resumen.texto: Navarrese who founded Pamplona (1549) and led campaigns against the Muzo and, in Panama, against the Bayano maroons. In 1560 he left Peru by the Amazon in search of Omagua and El Dorado, and he was murdered on January 1, 1561 by a conspiracy of his men in which Lope de Aguirre took part.

personas/lope-de-aguirre/resumen.texto: Soldier from Gipuzkoa who took part in Ursúa’s murder (1561), rebelled against Philip II, sailed down the Amazon, took Margarita Island and moved on to Venezuela, killing dozens of his own companions. Cornered in Barquisimeto in October 1561, he killed his daughter Elvira, and his own men then killed him, according to accounts of the expedition; his letter to the king is an exceptional document of conquistador rebelliousness.

personas/diego-de-losada/resumen.texto: Native of Zamora who in 1567 conquered the Caracas valley, defended by a coalition of caciques, and founded Santiago de León de Caracas.

personas/guaicaipuro/resumen.texto: Cacique of the Teques who led the resistance of the peoples of the Caracas valley to the Spanish in the 1560s and died around 1568 in a Spanish attack on his house. Almost everything known about him comes from the chronicle of Oviedo y Baños (1723), written a century and a half later.

personas/antonio-de-berrio/resumen.texto: Military officer married to a niece of Jiménez de Quesada, from whom he inherited the right to search for El Dorado. He made three expeditions up the Orinoco (1584-1591), governed Trinidad and Guayana, and in 1595 was captured by Walter Raleigh, whose accounts fed the idea of Manoa.

personas/walter-raleigh/resumen.texto: Courtier of Elizabeth I of England. In 1595 he took San José de Oruña in Trinidad, sailed up the Orinoco and published The Discoverie of Guiana (1596). On his second expedition (1617-1618) his men attacked Santo Tomé de Guayana, violating the peace with Spain, and he was executed in London on his return.

personas/gonzalo-suarez-rendon/resumen.texto: Captain of Jiménez de Quesada’s force who founded Tunja in 1539 on the site of Hunza, the seat of the zaque, and was one of its main encomenderos.

personas/juan-de-carvajal/resumen.texto: Interim governor of Venezuela who founded El Tocuyo (1545) and had Philipp von Hutten and Bartolomé Welser executed (1546). The judge Juan Pérez de Tolosa sentenced him to death and had him hanged that same year.

personas/juan-de-castellanos/resumen.texto: Andalusian who was a soldier and pearl diver in Cubagua before taking holy orders; he was a beneficed priest of Tunja for four decades. He wrote the Elegías de varones ilustres de Indias, considered the longest poem in the Castilian language, with testimonies from conquistadors he had known.

personas/pedro-de-aguado/resumen.texto: Franciscan who lived in the New Kingdom and wrote around 1575-1581 the Recopilación historial on the conquest of Santa Marta, the New Kingdom and Venezuela. It was not printed at the time and was published only in the 20th century.

personas/pedro-simon/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Cuenca, professor in Santafé, author of the Noticias historiales de las conquistas de Tierra Firme (first part, 1627). His work, which draws on Aguado and on witnesses, is the main source on Muisca religion and on the expedition of Ursúa and Aguirre.

personas/juan-rodriguez-freyle/resumen.texto: Creole of Santafé, soldier and farmer, author of El Carnero (1636-1638), a chronicle of the city’s scandals and lawsuits that includes the most cited description of the ceremony of the golden cacique at Guatavita.

personas/lucas-fernandez-de-piedrahita/r.texto: Creole of Santafé who was bishop of Santa Marta and of Panama. His Historia general de las conquistas del Nuevo Reino de Granada (1688) reworks Castellanos, Simón and the lost Compendio of Jiménez de Quesada.

personas/bernardo-de-lugo/resumen.texto: Dominican, professor of the Muisca language in Santafé, author of the first printed grammar of that language (Madrid, 1619).

personas/pedro-claver/resumen.texto: Catalan Jesuit who from 1610 attended in Cartagena to the Africans who arrived on slave ships, baptizing, treating and catechizing them with interpreters. When he took his final vows (1622) he signed “Petrus Claver, aethiopum semper servus” (“slave of the Blacks forever”); he did not condemn the slave trade as an institution. He was canonized in 1888.

personas/alonso-de-sandoval/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Seville raised in Lima, who spent almost his whole life in Cartagena. He interviewed newly arrived Africans and ship captains to write a treatise (1627) on their peoples, their languages and how to evangelize them, with explicit doubts about the justice of the slave trade.

personas/jose-gumilla/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Valencia, missionary in the Llanos of Casanare and the Orinoco and superior of those missions. His Orinoco ilustrado (1741) describes the peoples of the river, the Carib trade in captives and the nature of the basin.

personas/filippo-salvatore-gilij/resumen.texto: Italian Jesuit who was a missionary among the Tamanacos of the middle Orinoco for eighteen years. Expelled in 1767, he wrote in Rome the Saggio di storia americana, where he groups several languages into families according to their kinship, among them Carib and the one he called Maipure, today Arawakan.

personas/jose-celestino-mutis/resumen.texto: Physician from Cádiz who arrived in Cartagena in 1760 with Viceroy Messía de la Cerda and in Santafé at the start of 1761. He taught the Copernican system and the sciences of his time at the Colegio del Rosario, was ordained a priest, and from 1783 directed the Royal Botanical Expedition of the New Kingdom of Granada.

personas/francisco-jose-de-caldas/resume.texto: Native of Popayán who measured altitudes using the boiling point of water, directed the Santafé Observatory and edited the Semanario del Nuevo Reino de Granada (1808-1810). He joined the patriot cause as a military engineer and was shot on Morillo’s orders in 1816.

personas/jose-de-oviedo-y-banos/resumen.texto: Bogotá-born man raised in Lima who settled in Caracas, where he was an alderman (regidor). His Historia de la conquista y población de la provincia de Venezuela (1723) is the main source on Guaicaipuro and the founding of Caracas, written a century and a half after the events with documents from the cabildo.

personas/benkos-bioho/resumen.texto: Enslaved African (Domingo Biohó in the Spanish documents) who fled Cartagena around 1599 and led a palenque in the Matuna hills. He negotiated truces with the governors and was hanged in 1621. Tradition makes him the founder of San Basilio de Palenque, a link the documents do not prove.

personas/coffy/resumen.texto: Enslaved man of Akan (coromantí) origin, a cooper on a Berbice plantation, who in 1763 led the largest slave rebellion in Dutch Guiana. He proposed in a letter to the governor that the colony be divided; after the rebels split, he took his own life. Guyana regards him as a national hero.

personas/jose-leonardo-chirino/resumen.texto: Free zambo, son of an enslaved man and an Indigenous woman, who worked for a merchant in Coro and had travelled to Saint-Domingue. In May 1795 he led an uprising of enslaved people and free people that demanded the abolition of slavery and of tribute, invoking the “law of the French”; he was captured, hanged and quartered in Caracas in 1796.

personas/john-gabriel-stedman/resumen.texto: Scottish-Dutch officer who served in Suriname between 1772 and 1777 in the campaigns against the Boni maroons. His Narrative (1796), with engravings, some by William Blake, showed in detail the punishments of enslaved people and was used by British abolitionism.

personas/blas-de-lezo/resumen.texto: Naval officer from Gipuzkoa, commander of the Cartagena naval station, who with Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava directed the defense against the British attack of 1741. He died in the city shortly afterward, probably of an epidemic disease. He was greatly celebrated in Spain in the 21st century.

personas/edward-vernon/resumen.texto: British admiral who took Portobelo in 1739 and in 1741 led the great expedition against Cartagena de Indias, which failed with thousands dead, mostly from disease.

personas/francisco-moreno-y-escandon/res.texto: Crown prosecutor of the Audiencia of Santafé, born in Mariquita. He proposed an enlightened curriculum (1774), opened the Royal Public Library with books from the expelled Jesuits (1777) and, as inspector (visitador, 1778-1779), merged and auctioned off the resguardos, the Indigenous communal lands, that he considered depopulated.

personas/antonio-caballero-y-gongora/res.texto: Archbishop of Santafé who negotiated with the comuneros and signed the Capitulations of Zipaquirá (1781), which the government then annulled. As viceroy (1782-1789) he supported the Botanical Expedition and the reform of studies.

personas/jose-antonio-galan/resumen.texto: Mestizo from Charalá who carried on the comunero rebellion after the Capitulations of Zipaquirá and raised enslaved people and Indigenous people in the Magdalena valley. He was hanged and quartered in Santafé on February 1, 1782; his head and limbs were displayed in several towns.

personas/manuela-beltran/resumen.texto: Resident of El Socorro to whom tradition attributes tearing up the edict of new taxes on March 16, 1781, a gesture taken as the start of the comunero rebellion. Documents of the period say very little about her: her exact role, and even her birth date (1724 or 1750, depending on the sources), are uncertain.

personas/antonio-narino/resumen.texto: Creole of Santafé, treasurer of tithes and owner of a printing press, who in 1793-1794 translated and printed the Rights of Man and was sentenced to ten years in a presidio in Africa. He presided over the state of Cundinamarca (1811-1813), in conflict with the federalists, and was captured by the royalists in the southern campaign (1814).

personas/francisco-de-miranda/resumen.texto: Native of Caracas who was a Spanish officer, a general in the French Revolution and a promoter in London of Spanish American independence. He landed at Coro in 1806 without local support, returned in 1810, signed the act of 1811 and, as dictator of the First Republic, capitulated in 1812; handed over to the Spanish, he died in prison in Cádiz.

personas/camilo-torres-tenorio/resumen.texto: Lawyer from Popayán, author of the Memorial de agravios (1809) and leader of the federalists of the United Provinces of New Granada, which he presided over. He was shot on Morillo’s orders in 1816.

personas/policarpa-salavarrieta/resumen.texto: Seamstress from Guaduas who passed information and recruits to the patriot guerrillas of the Llanos during the Spanish reconquest. She was shot in Santafé on November 14, 1817 and became a symbol of Colombian independence.

personas/francisco-de-paula-santander/re.texto: Military officer from Cúcuta who organized the army of the Llanos in 1818-1819 and fought at Boyacá. He was vice president of Gran Colombia in charge of the government while Bolívar waged the southern war, and later president of New Granada (1832-1837).

personas/jose-antonio-paez/resumen.texto: Chief of the llaneros of Apure, many of whom had fought for the king with Boves and in 1816-1818 switched to the patriot cause. He fought at Carabobo (1821), led in 1826 the La Cosiata movement against Bogotá, and in 1830 became the first president of separate Venezuela.

personas/jose-tomas-boves/resumen.texto: Asturian merchant in the Llanos who in 1813-1814 raised for the king an army of pardo llaneros and enslaved people with promises of plunder and freedom. He defeated Bolívar at La Puerta (1814) and destroyed the Second Republic; his troops and the patriots killed prisoners and civilians. He died in Urica in December 1814.

personas/pablo-morillo/resumen.texto: Spanish general who commanded the expedition of some 10,000 men sent in 1815 to reconquer Venezuela and New Granada. He besieged and took Cartagena (1815), and in Santafé he set up tribunals that sentenced dozens of patriot leaders to death (1816); in 1820 he signed with Bolívar the armistice and the treaty regularizing the war.

personas/konrad-theodor-preuss/resumen.texto: German ethnologist who excavated San Agustín in 1913-1914 and published the first systematic description of its statuary (1929); he also studied the Kogi of the Sierra Nevada.

personas/gerardo-reichel-dolmatoff/resum.texto: Austrian-born anthropologist naturalized as Colombian, founder of scientific archaeology in the country: he excavated Puerto Hormiga, San Agustín and Tairona sites and studied the Kogi and the Desana. After his death his past as a Nazi militant in Austria in the 1930s came to light.

personas/juan-friede/resumen.texto: Ukrainian-Colombian historian who published much of the Archivo de Indias documents on the conquest of the New Kingdom and studied the Welser governorship in Venezuela and Indigenous resistance.

personas/john-leddy-phelan/resumen.texto: American historian of Spanish America. In The People and the King (1978, posthumous) he interpreted the comunero revolt as a defense of an “unwritten constitution” of negotiation with the Crown, and not as a precursor of independence.

personas/carl-henrik-langebaek/resumen.texto: Colombian archaeologist, professor at the Universidad de los Andes, who studied the Muisca chiefdoms through regional excavations and critical reading of the chronicles, and questioned the image of a centralized Muisca “confederation.”

personas/neil-l-whitehead/resumen.texto: British anthropologist who studied the history of the Caribs of the Orinoco and the Guianas (Lords of the Tiger Spirit, 1988), Indigenous warfare and ritual violence, and who critically edited Raleigh’s Discoverie of Guiana.

hechos/cultura-san-agustin/resumen.texto: Agricultural societies of the upper Magdalena who, during the first millennium AD, buried their principal dead in tombs and mounds accompanied by stone statues of human and animal figures, many with feline fangs. They left no writing, and it is not known what language they spoke or what they called themselves; whether the statues represent guardians, shamans or ancestors is a matter of interpretation.

hechos/cultura-calima/resumen.texto: Succession of societies of the Calima River valley, in the Western Cordillera, which archaeologists call Ilama, Yotoco and Sonso. They are known for their goldwork (diadems, nose ornaments and pectorals), their shaft tombs and their raised-field and terrace farming; the dates of each period vary by author.

hechos/cultura-quimbaya/resumen.texto: Archaeologists distinguish in the middle Cauca valley an early Quimbaya period, from the first millennium AD, to which the most famous gold and tumbaga pieces belong, and a late one, whose population Jorge Robledo encountered in 1539. The name Quimbaya, of a 16th-century people, was later applied to all the goldwork of the region, although the classic pieces are centuries older.

hechos/tesoro-de-los-quimbayas/titulo.texto: Discovery and Gift of the Quimbaya Treasure

hechos/tesoro-de-los-quimbayas/resumen.texto: Grave goods from two tombs of the early Quimbaya period, found by guaqueros (grave robbers) around 1890-1891 near Filandia; much of the pieces were sold to private buyers or melted down. The government of Carlos Holguín bought more than a hundred gold and tumbaga pieces, exhibited them in Madrid in 1892 and gave them to Queen Regent María Cristina; they are in the Museo de América. In 2017 Colombia’s Constitutional Court ordered steps to secure their return, and in 2024 the government formally requested it from Spain.

hechos/cultura-zenu/titulo.texto: Zenú and the San Jorge Canals

hechos/cultura-zenu/resumen.texto: The ancestors of the Zenú built, on the floodplains of the San Jorge and Sinú rivers, between roughly the 2nd century BC and the 10th century AD, a system of canals and raised fields covering hundreds of thousands of hectares, studied by Clemencia Plazas and Ana María Falchetti. When the Spanish arrived they were divided into three provinces (Finzenú, Panzenú and Zenúfana), and their burial mounds with gold drew the looting of Pedro de Heredia.

hechos/cultura-tairona/resumen.texto: Societies of the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta who built villages with terraces, paved roads and stone channels, and worked gold and tumbaga. Archaeologists distinguish a Nahuange period (up to the 10th century) and a Tairona period. They resisted the Spanish from Santa Marta for almost a century; the present-day Kogi, Arhuaco, Wiwa and Kankuamo are considered their heirs.

hechos/confederacion-muisca/resumen.texto: The Muiscas, who spoke a Chibchan language, lived on the highlands of Cundinamarca and Boyacá. Estimates of their number when the Spanish arrived vary widely according to author and method, from several hundred thousand to two million. They were organized into chiefdoms grouped around the zipa of Bacatá and the zaque of Hunza, and the lordships of Sugamuxi (seat of the iraca, the religious leader) and Tundama, and traded salt, cotton mantles, emeralds and gold. Chroniclers described them as a monarchy or “confederation”; archaeologists such as Langebaek hold that they were a set of chiefdoms without a centralized state.

hechos/guerras-entre-zipas-y-zaques/titu.texto: Wars between the Zipas and the Zaques

hechos/guerras-entre-zipas-y-zaques/resu.texto: According to Simón and Piedrahita, the zipas of Bacatá subjected neighboring chiefdoms (Fusagasugá, Ubaté, Guatavita) and waged war with the zaques of Hunza; in the battle of Chocontá, around 1490, the zipa Saguamanchica and the zaque Michuá are said to have died. These chronologies were reconstructed from traditions collected between half a century and a century and a half later, and their dates and details are uncertain.

hechos/sacrificio-humano-muisca/resumen.texto: Chroniclers describe the sacrifice of the moxas: children bought or captured in the Llanos, raised in the shrines and sacrificed to the Sun around puberty, with their blood offered in temples such as the one at Sogamoso. They also mention the killing of war captives and the burial of women and servants with the caciques. Almost all of this comes from Simón and Piedrahita, who wrote 80 to 150 years later; direct archaeological evidence is scarce and the scale cannot be confirmed.

hechos/guerras-entre-muiscas-y-panches/t.texto: Wars between the Muiscas and the Panches

hechos/guerras-entre-muiscas-y-panches/r.texto: The Panches, from the temperate lands west of the highlands, waged constant war against the Muiscas, who garrisoned their frontier. Chroniclers accuse them of eating their enemies, an accusation that served to justify their conquest and that has no independent confirmation. In August 1538 Spaniards and warriors of the zipa Sagipa defeated them together at Tocarema.

hechos/pueblo-caquetio/resumen.texto: Arawakan-speaking people of the Falcón coast, of Aruba, Curaçao and Bonaire, and of the Barinas llanos. In 1515 the Spanish deported those of Curaçao to Hispaniola as slaves, considering the islands “useless”; in 1527 their lord Manaure made a pact with Juan de Ampíes, and the Welsers relied on them as allies and carriers.

hechos/timoto-cuicas/resumen.texto: Peoples of the Venezuelan Andes (Mérida and Trujillo) who farmed on irrigated terraces, stored their harvests in underground storehouses and had shrines at lagoons and caves. Their organization and language are poorly known; the Spanish subjected them from the founding of Mérida in 1558.

hechos/caribes-del-orinoco/titulo.texto: Caribs (Kari’ña) of the Orinoco and the Guianas

hechos/caribes-del-orinoco/resumen.texto: Carib-speaking people of the lower Orinoco and the Guiana coast. In the 17th and 18th centuries they raided upriver, captured women and children of other peoples (the poitos) and exchanged them with the Dutch of the Essequibo for tools, cloth and weapons, a trade documented by Gumilla and the Dutch archives. A royal cédula of 1503 allowed the enslavement of “cannibals”; according to Whitehead, the label “Carib” was applied more to those who resisted the Spanish than to those who ate human flesh.

hechos/pueblo-wayuu/resumen.texto: Arawakan-speaking people of the Guajira peninsula, organized in matrilineal clans. They quickly adopted European cattle, horses and firearms, traded with the English and Dutch, and were never fully subjected by Spain.

hechos/rebelion-guajira-de-1769/resumen.texto: In May 1769 the Wayuu rose up against the Spanish authorities of the Guajira, attacked villages, haciendas and missions, and forced troops to be sent from Riohacha and Cartagena. The campaigns failed to subdue them, and the peninsula remained outside Spain’s effective control until the end of the colony.

hechos/balsa-muisca/resumen.texto: Gold votive figure (tunjo) from the Muisca period showing a chief with his retinue on a raft, found in 1969 in a cave in Pasca and held in the Museo del Oro. It is related to the Guatavita ceremony described by Rodríguez Freyle; a similar piece found at Siecha in 1856 was lost in a fire in Germany.

hechos/viaje-de-ojeda-de-1499/titulo.texto: Voyage of Ojeda, La Cosa and Vespucci to the Venezuelan Coast

hechos/viaje-de-ojeda-de-1499/resumen.texto: First expedition authorized to follow the route of Columbus’s third voyage: in 1499 it explored the coast from the Gulf of Paria to the Guajira, passing Margarita, Curaçao and Lake Maracaibo, and carried off captured Indigenous people to sell. The name Venezuela is explained by the stilt houses on the lake, which recalled Venice; Martín Fernández de Enciso wrote in 1519 that it was an Indigenous name.

hechos/viaje-de-bastidas/titulo.texto: Voyage of Rodrigo de Bastidas and Juan de la Cosa

hechos/viaje-de-bastidas/resumen.texto: Bastidas, with Juan de la Cosa as pilot and Vasco Núñez de Balboa among his men, explored in 1501 the Caribbean coast of present-day Colombia from Cabo de la Vela to the Gulf of Urabá and Darién, trading gold and pearls with the Indigenous people.

hechos/gobernacion-de-ojeda-y-uraba/titu.texto: Ojeda’s Expeditions in Urabá and the Death of Juan de la Cosa

hechos/gobernacion-de-ojeda-y-uraba/resu.texto: In 1508 Ojeda received the governorship of New Andalusia. In 1509-1510 his force attacked Calamarí and Turbaco, where the Indigenous people, using poisoned arrows, killed Juan de la Cosa and much of the Spanish force; Ojeda then founded San Sebastián de Urabá, abandoned that same year. The survivors, with Enciso and Balboa, founded Santa María la Antigua del Darién.

hechos/pesca-de-perlas-de-cubagua/titulo.texto: Pearl Fishing at Cubagua and the Enslavement of Indigenous People

hechos/pesca-de-perlas-de-cubagua/resume.texto: From the early 16th century the Spanish exploited the pearl beds of Cubagua, Margarita and the coast of Cumaná with Indigenous divers, first Lucayans brought from the Bahamas and then captured on the Tierra Firme coast on the argument that they were Caribs. Las Casas described the diving expeditions and the deaths in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies; the pearl beds were exhausted by about 1540.

hechos/misiones-de-cumana-y-colonia-de-l.texto: Missions of Cumaná and Las Casas’s Colony

Franciscans and Dominicans founded convents from 1513-1515 on the coast of Cumaná and at Chiribichí to evangelize without conquest. Spanish slave raids from Cubagua provoked Indigenous reprisals: in 1520 the Chiribichí convent was destroyed and Gonzalo de Ocampo led a punitive expedition. Las Casas, who had obtained in 1520 a capitulation to colonize peacefully with farmers, saw his settlement fail in 1522 after a new attack, and soon afterward became a Dominican friar.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-marta/resumen.texto: Rodrigo de Bastidas founded Santa Marta on July 29, 1525 with a license to settle and trade. He forbade attacks on peaceful peoples, and in 1526 his own captains stabbed him; his successors carried out raids of plunder against the Tairona and other peoples of the Sierra, which Las Casas denounced in A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies.

hechos/fundacion-de-coro/resumen.texto: Juan de Ampíes, factor of the Audiencia of Santo Domingo, founded Santa Ana de Coro in July 1527 after making a pact with the Caquetío chief Manaure, with the declared aim of curbing slave captures on the coast. The following year the province was handed over to the Welsers and Coro became its capital.

hechos/concesion-de-los-welser/resumen.texto: Under the 1528 capitulation Charles V handed the province of Venezuela to the factors of the Welsers, bankers of Augsburg who had lent him large sums. Tradition presents it as payment of that debt, although the document is a conquest capitulation like those signed with private Spaniards. Their German and Spanish governors devoted the governorship to expeditions in search of gold and El Dorado, in which they captured and sold Indigenous people as slaves to finance them; Las Casas accused the Germans of extreme cruelties. After the execution of Hutten (1546) the Crown took over the government, and in 1556 the contract (asiento) was ended.

hechos/entradas-de-ehinger/resumen.texto: Ehinger founded Maracaibo (1529) and in two expeditions explored the lake, the Perijá range, the Cesar valley down to the Magdalena and the highlands of Pamplona, plundering villages and taking Indigenous people in chains as carriers, many of whom died; the sale of captives helped pay for the enterprise. He died in 1533, wounded by a poisoned arrow.

hechos/entradas-de-federmann/resumen.texto: On his first expedition (1530-1531) Federmann marched from Coro southward through the lands of the Caquetíos and Jirajaras; on the second (1536-1539) he crossed the Llanos and the Eastern Cordillera and reached the Bogotá savanna in 1539, with few survivors from his force and from his Indigenous carriers.

hechos/fundacion-de-cartagena-de-indias/.texto: Pedro de Heredia founded Cartagena on June 1, 1533 next to the village of Calamarí, after fighting with the peoples of the bay and of Turbaco. The expeditions of the first years, in search of gold from the Zenú tombs, financed the city, which later became a port of call for the Tierra Firme fleet and one of the main ports of the African slave trade.

hechos/saqueo-de-las-tumbas-del-sinu/tit.texto: Looting of the Zenú Tombs of the Sinú

hechos/saqueo-de-las-tumbas-del-sinu/res.texto: In 1534 Pedro de Heredia and his men entered Finzenú and looted the Zenú burial mounds, from which they took an amount of gold that the chroniclers describe as enormous. The division of the booty and the accusations of fraud against the royal fifth (quinto real) were part of the residency trial brought against Heredia in 1536.

hechos/conquista-del-territorio-muisca/r.texto: In April 1536 Jiménez de Quesada left Santa Marta with some 800 men and went up the Magdalena; in March 1537 between 160 and 180 reached the highlands, according to the sources, after losing most of them to hunger, disease and attacks. Taking advantage of the rivalries between the zipa, the zaque and minor caciques, and with Indigenous allies, they took Hunza (August 1537), plundered Sogamoso and other shrines, and over three years subjected the main lordships. The caciques were distributed in encomiendas among the conquistadors.

hechos/incendio-del-templo-de-sogamoso/t.texto: Fire at the Temple of the Sun at Sogamoso

hechos/incendio-del-templo-de-sogamoso/l.texto: Temple of the Sun at Sogamoso

hechos/incendio-del-templo-de-sogamoso/r.texto: In September 1537 the force entered Sogamoso at night, seat of the iraca. According to the chronicles, two soldiers looting the temple with torches set it on fire by accident, and it burned for days. The chroniclers lament above all the gold that was lost; the episode later became a symbol of the destruction of the Muisca religious world.

hechos/muerte-de-sagipa/resumen.texto: Sagipa, successor of Tisquesusa and ally of the Spanish against the Panches, was arrested at the end of 1538 for refusing to hand over his predecessor’s treasure; he was tortured and died in prison at the beginning of 1539. In the trial brought against him in Spain, Jiménez de Quesada was accused of this death, and the testimony from that case is one of the main sources on the episode.

hechos/fundacion-de-bogota/resumen.texto: Jiménez de Quesada founded Santafé on August 6, 1538 at Teusaquillo, a resting place of the zipa. The formal establishment with a cabildo took place in April 1539, after the arrival of the forces of Federmann and Belalcázar.

hechos/encuentro-de-quesada-federmann-y-.texto: Meeting of Jiménez de Quesada, Federmann and Belalcázar

In early 1539 two other forces reached the Bogotá savanna almost at the same time, where Jiménez de Quesada had been since 1537: that of Sebastián de Belalcázar from Quito and that of Federmann from Venezuela. Instead of fighting, they agreed to take the dispute over the governorship of the New Kingdom to the Council of the Indies and traveled together to Spain.

hechos/ejecucion-de-aquiminzaque/titulo.texto: Execution of Aquiminzaque and the Caciques of Tunja

hechos/ejecucion-de-aquiminzaque/resumen.texto: Hernán Pérez de Quesada, who governed the New Kingdom, had the zaque Aquiminzaque and other caciques accused of plotting an uprising beheaded in Tunja in 1540, a conspiracy known only from Spanish sources. With these executions the resistance of the northern lordships ended.

hechos/leyenda-de-el-dorado/resumen.texto: The report of a chief who covered himself with gold dust to make offerings in a lake circulated among the conquistadors from the 1530s and was linked to the Muisca ceremony at Guatavita that Rodríguez Freyle described a century later. The “golden Indian” became a kingdom or a city (Omagua, Manoa) that kept moving into the unknown and drew expeditions by Belalcázar, Hutten, Pérez de Quesada, Ursúa, Jiménez de Quesada, Berrío and Raleigh, with heavy losses of Spanish and Indigenous lives. No such city existed: what existed was a highly developed ritual goldwork and gold offerings in lakes.

hechos/jornada-de-ursua-y-aguirre/titulo.texto: Expedition of Ursúa and Lope de Aguirre

hechos/jornada-de-ursua-y-aguirre/resume.texto: Expedition organized by the viceroy of Peru to search for Omagua and El Dorado and to occupy idle soldiers; from September 1560 it went down the Huallaga and the Amazon with some 300 Spaniards and hundreds of Indigenous people. On January 1, 1561 a conspiracy killed Ursúa; Lope de Aguirre took control, had dozens of companions killed, reached the Atlantic, took Margarita Island and landed in Venezuela, where his men abandoned him and killed him in Barquisimeto on October 27, 1561.

hechos/conquista-del-valle-de-caracas/ti.texto: Conquest of the Caracas Valley and Founding of the City

hechos/conquista-del-valle-de-caracas/re.texto: In the 1560s the caciques of the Caracas valley, among them Guaicaipuro, rejected the first Spanish settlements. Diego de Losada entered in 1567 and founded Santiago de León de Caracas; resistance continued until Guaicaipuro’s death around 1568 and the capture of other caciques. The detailed account is that of Oviedo y Baños, from 1723.

hechos/viajes-de-raleigh-a-guayana/resum.texto: In 1595 Raleigh took San José de Oruña in Trinidad, captured the governor Antonio de Berrío and sailed up the Orinoco to the Caroní in search of Manoa, allying with caciques hostile to the Spanish. In 1617 he returned with the permission of James I on condition that he not attack the Spanish; his men, under Lawrence Keymis, assaulted Santo Tomé de Guayana, where his son died, and on his return he was beheaded in London (1618).

hechos/audiencia-de-santafe/titulo.texto: Royal Audiencia of Santafé and Kingdom of New Granada

hechos/audiencia-de-santafe/resumen.texto: The Crown created in 1549 an Audiencia in Santafé, installed in 1550, which governed the Kingdom of New Granada, with presidents from 1564. Its oidores visited the Indian towns, assessed encomienda tribute and applied, against the resistance of the encomenderos, the New Laws (1542) and the 1549 cédula that prohibited collecting tribute in personal service.

hechos/encomienda-y-despoblacion-del-nue.texto: Encomienda, Forced Labor and the Decline of the Indigenous Population in the New Kingdom

After the conquest, Muiscas and other peoples were distributed in encomiendas that collected tribute and personal services. They were also obliged to work in rotations in the silver mines of Mariquita and the emerald mines of Muzo, and as rowers on the Magdalena, labor with very high mortality that the Crown prohibited several times. Smallpox epidemics in 1558 and 1587-1590, labor and displacement caused the population to fall: the tribute-payer counts of the inspections, studied by Germán Colmenares and others, show a sharp decline until the mid-17th century, less extreme than in the Caribbean lowlands, where whole peoples disappeared.

hechos/resguardos-indigenas/titulo.texto: Indigenous Resguardos of the New Kingdom

hechos/resguardos-indigenas/resumen.texto: From the 1590s the oidores of the Audiencia of Santafé, on their visits, assigned to each Indian town communal lands that could not be sold, the resguardos, and concentrated the scattered population in towns with a church. They protected a land base against landowners while also freeing land for the Spanish. In the 18th century, with fewer Indigenous people and more mestizos, the inspector Moreno y Escandón merged and auctioned off many (1778); the republic ordered them divided, although some survived and the Colombian Constitution recognizes them today.

hechos/fundacion-del-hospital-de-santafe.texto: Hospital de San Juan de Dios de Santafé

Fray Juan de los Barrios, first archbishop of Santafé, founded a hospital in the city in 1564; in the 17th century it passed to the Brothers Hospitallers of Saint John of God and for more than four centuries it was the city’s main hospital.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-santo.texto: Bull Authorizing a Dominican Estudio General in Santafé
Universidad de Santo Tomás de Santafé

A bull of Gregory XIII of 1580 authorized the Dominicans of Santafé to have an estudio general with the power to confer degrees. That power took decades to put into practice; the present-day Universidad Santo Tomás claims that date as its founding.

hechos/rebelion-tairona-de-1599/resumen.texto: In 1599 several Tairona villages of the Sierra Nevada rose up against the encomenderos of Santa Marta. According to Pedro Simón, Governor Juan Guiral Velón defeated them in 1600, executed their leaders and burned their villages; the survivors withdrew to the high parts of the sierra, where their descendants live.

hechos/guerra-de-los-pijaos/resumen.texto: The Pijao, peoples of the Central Cordillera (Tolima and Huila), attacked Spanish towns and roads for half a century. The Spanish accused them of cannibalism, which allowed them to enslave them. From 1605 Juan de Borja, president of the Audiencia, waged a systematic war against them, with help from the Coyaima and Natagaima, which ended in their defeat; the survivors were relocated and distributed.

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-en-cartagena/ti.texto: Cartagena, Port of the African Slave Trade

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-en-cartagena/re.texto: From the late 16th century Cartagena was, together with Veracruz, one of the ports authorized for the entry of enslaved Africans into Spanish America, and during the Portuguese asientos (1595-1640) tens of thousands of people came through it. They were sold for the mines of the New Kingdom and Popayán, the haciendas, urban services and Peru. Sandoval and Claver described the state in which they arrived and the mortality on the ships and in the city’s holding depots.

hechos/palenques-de-cartagena/resumen.texto: From the late 16th century Africans fleeing Cartagena formed palenques in the Matuna and María hills. One was led by Domingo (Benkos) Biohó, who negotiated truces with the governors and was hanged in 1621; campaigns against the palenques continued throughout the 17th century. At the beginning of the 18th century Bishop Antonio María Casiani negotiated the reducción of San Basilio, with pardon and recognition of their freedom.

hechos/tribunal-de-la-inquisicion-de-car.texto: Palace of the Inquisition in Cartagena

Third American tribunal of the Holy Office, created in 1610 with jurisdiction over the New Kingdom, Venezuela, Panama and the Antilles. Indigenous people were exempt from the Inquisition; the tribunal judged mostly blasphemy, sorcery, African religious practices, bigamy and Portuguese conversos accused of Judaizing. Death sentences were few, while penances, whippings and confiscations were frequent; the juntas abolished it in 1811, it was re-established in 1815 and it disappeared in 1821.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-javeriana/resumen.texto: The Jesuits of Santafé, who had directed the Colegio de San Bartolomé since 1604, obtained in 1623 the power to confer university degrees, the origin of the Universidad Javeriana; it operated until the expulsion of 1767.

hechos/fundacion-del-colegio-del-rosario.texto: Founding of the Colegio Mayor del Rosario
Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario

The Dominican archbishop Cristóbal de Torres founded in 1653 the Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario, with constitutions taken from the Colegio Mayor del Arzobispo in Salamanca, to train letrados (learned men) of the New Kingdom in philosophy, theology and law.

hechos/misiones-jesuitas-de-los-llanos-y.texto: Jesuit Missions of the Llanos and the Orinoco

From 1661 the Jesuits founded reducciones in the Llanos of Casanare and the Meta with Achagua, Sáliba, Betoye and other peoples, and from the 1730s on in the middle Orinoco, protected by armed escorts against the Caribs and Dutch traders. They introduced cattle and crops, wrote grammars of the local languages and suffered repeated epidemics; after the expulsion of 1767 they passed to other religious orders and many were depopulated.

hechos/mineria-del-oro-con-esclavos-en-e.texto: Gold Mining with Enslaved Africans in the Pacific

After subjugating the peoples of Chocó at the end of the 17th century, miners from Popayán and Antioquia brought gangs of enslaved Africans to the Pacific rivers, which in the 18th century produced much of the viceroyalty’s gold. That population, enslaved and free, is the origin of the Afro-Colombian communities of the Pacific.

hechos/fundacion-de-la-universidad-de-ca.texto: Founding of the University of Caracas
Royal and Pontifical University of Caracas
A royal cédula of Philip V dated December 22, 1721 elevated the seminary of Santa Rosa in Caracas to a university, with papal confirmation in 1722; university courses began in 1725.

hechos/compania-guipuzcoana/resumen.texto: Company of Basque merchants that received in 1728 the monopoly on trade between Venezuela and Spain, above all cacao, with the task of combating Dutch smuggling from Curaçao. Creole growers and merchants accused it of paying low prices; in 1749 the Canary Islander Juan Francisco de León led an uprising against it. It lost the monopoly and was dissolved in 1785.

hechos/virreinato-de-nueva-granada/resum.texto: Created in 1717 with the audiencias of Santafé, Quito and Panama and the province of Venezuela, suppressed in 1723 because of its cost and re-established in 1739. Its viceroys sought to defend the coast against the British and against smuggling, to increase revenues (state monopolies on aguardiente and tobacco) and to promote gold mining; Venezuela had its own government from 1742 and formed the Captaincy General in 1777.

hechos/primera-imprenta-de-santafe/resum.texto: The Jesuits set up the first permanent printing press of the New Kingdom in Santafé, from which around 1738 came the city’s first known printed book, a devotional work. Others followed, such as the one in Cartagena and, in the 1790s, the Patriotic Press of Nariño. Printing reached Caracas only in 1808, when the Gazeta de Caracas began to be published.

hechos/ataque-de-vernon-a-cartagena/titu.texto: British Attack on Cartagena de Indias

hechos/ataque-de-vernon-a-cartagena/resu.texto: Between March and May 1741, during the War of the Asiento, a British expedition under Edward Vernon and Thomas Wentworth, with some 180 ships and more than 20,000 men, including colonists from North America and enslaved people from Jamaica, besieged Cartagena. It took the defenses of Bocachica but failed before the San Felipe castle, defended by the troops of Viceroy Sebastián de Eslava and Blas de Lezo; the British lost between 9,500 and 11,500 men, most of them to yellow fever and other diseases. With the first reports of success, medals were minted in England celebrating a capture of the city that never happened.

hechos/real-biblioteca-de-santafe/titulo.texto: Opening of the Royal Public Library of Santafé

hechos/real-biblioteca-de-santafe/resume.texto: With books confiscated from the Jesuits expelled in 1767, the crown prosecutor Moreno y Escandón organized a public library that opened in 1777, the origin of the National Library of Colombia.

hechos/capitania-general-de-venezuela/re.texto: By royal cédula of September 8, 1777 Charles III placed under the captain general of Caracas the provinces of Venezuela, Cumaná, Guayana, Maracaibo, Trinidad and Margarita, which had already shared an intendancy since 1776; in 1786 the Royal Audiencia of Caracas was created. It is the territorial base of present-day Venezuela.

hechos/real-expedicion-botanica/titulo.texto: Royal Botanical Expedition of the New Kingdom of Granada

hechos/real-expedicion-botanica/resumen.texto: Scientific enterprise approved in 1783 by Archbishop-Viceroy Caballero y Góngora and by Charles III, directed by Mutis from Mariquita and later from Santafé. It inventoried and painted the flora, sought useful plants such as cinchona, trained Creole naturalists and draftsmen such as Caldas, Zea and Lozano, and built an observatory. After Mutis’s death and the war, Morillo sent its collections to Madrid in 1816, and several of its members were shot.

hechos/revolucion-de-los-comuneros/resum.texto: On March 16, 1781, in El Socorro, a crowd tore up the edict of new taxes issued by the regent visitor Gutiérrez de Piñeres. The protest spread to dozens of towns, and some 20,000 comuneros, with Indigenous people of the savanna led by Ambrosio Pisco, marched toward Santafé; Archbishop Caballero y Góngora negotiated the Capitulations of Zipaquirá, which were later disavowed, and the repression focused on Galán and other leaders. Phelan interpreted it as a defense of a pact with the Crown; nationalist historiography saw it as a precursor of independence.
