hechos/ejecucion-de-galan/resumen.texto: On February 1, 1782 the Audiencia had Galán and three other comuneros hanged in Santafé. Their bodies were quartered, their heads and limbs displayed in the towns of the rebellion, their houses destroyed and their descendants declared infamous.

hechos/insurreccion-de-chirino/resumen.texto: On May 10, 1795, in the Sierra of Coro, enslaved people, free pardos and Indigenous people led by Chirino and José Caridad González rose up demanding the abolition of slavery and of tribute and the “law of the French”; they killed several hacendados and marched on Coro. They were defeated within a few days; many died in the repression or were executed without trial, and Chirino was hanged in 1796.

hechos/conspiracion-de-gual-y-espana/res.texto: Conspiracy uncovered in La Guaira in July 1797, inspired by the French Revolution and by the Spanish republican Juan Bautista Picornell, who was imprisoned there. Its program proclaimed equality among whites, Indigenous people, pardos and Blacks, the abolition of slavery and tribute, and free trade. José María España was hanged and quartered in Caracas in 1799; Manuel Gual died in Trinidad in 1800.

hechos/viaje-de-humboldt-por-venezuela/t.texto: Humboldt and Bonpland’s Journey through Venezuela and the Orinoco

hechos/viaje-de-humboldt-por-venezuela/r.texto: Humboldt and Bonpland arrived in Cumaná in July 1799 and in 1800 went up the Apure, the Orinoco, the Atabapo and the Río Negro, and returned by the Casiquiare, whose link between the Orinoco and Amazon basins they confirmed. They described the missions, Indigenous villages, curare and slavery on the haciendas, and in 1801 passed through New Granada, where they visited Mutis in Santafé.

hechos/expedicion-de-miranda-de-1806/res.texto: Miranda, with ships chartered in New York and British protection in the Caribbean, failed in April 1806 off Ocumare, where the Spanish captured two schooners and hanged ten of his men. In August he landed at La Vela de Coro and raised the tricolor flag, but the population did not support him and he withdrew within a few days.

hechos/colonia-de-esequibo-y-berbice/tit.texto: Dutch Colonies of Essequibo, Berbice and Demerara

hechos/colonia-de-esequibo-y-berbice/res.texto: Zeeland merchants established posts from the early 17th century on the Essequibo and on the Berbice (1627) to trade dyes, timber and captives with Indigenous peoples, and later sugar plantations worked by African slaves. In the mid-18th century Demerara was opened to British settlers; Great Britain occupied the three colonies during the wars with France and kept them in 1814, and in 1831 they formed British Guiana.

hechos/colonia-de-surinam/titulo.texto: Suriname: From English to Dutch Colony

hechos/colonia-de-surinam/resumen.texto: In 1650 Francis Willoughby founded an English colony of sugar plantations worked by African slaves on the Suriname River, where Sephardic Jews also settled. In February 1667 a Zeeland fleet under Abraham Crijnssen took it, and the Peace of Breda left it to the Dutch; from 1683 it was administered by the Society of Suriname.

hechos/esclavitud-en-surinam/resumen.texto: In the 18th century Suriname had hundreds of plantations of sugar, coffee, cacao and cotton worked by enslaved Africans, who were the great majority of the population. The punishments (whipping, mutilation and execution for flight or rebellion) are recorded in the colony’s ordinances and in accounts such as Stedman’s. Slavery was abolished on July 1, 1863, followed by ten more years of compulsory labor under state supervision; the date is commemorated as Keti Koti.

hechos/cimarrones-de-surinam/titulo.texto: Wars with the Suriname Maroons and Peace Treaties

hechos/cimarrones-de-surinam/resumen.texto: From the late 17th century thousands of Africans fled the plantations into the forest and formed villages that raided plantations in search of relatives, tools and weapons. Military expeditions failed, and the colony made peace with the Ndyuka (1760), the Saramaka (1762) and the Matawai (1767); against the Boni (Aluku) groups the war continued until they withdrew to French Guiana at the end of the century.

hechos/rebelion-de-berbice/resumen.texto: In late February 1763 (Guyana commemorates the 23rd) enslaved people on the plantations of the Dutch colony of Berbice rose up under Coffy and came to control almost the whole colony. Coffy proposed to Governor Van Hoogenheim that it be divided; divisions among the rebels, troops arriving from Europe and other colonies, and help from Carib and Arawak Indigenous people crushed the rebellion in 1764, with numerous executions.

hechos/expedicion-de-kourou/resumen.texto: After losing Canada, France sent more than ten thousand settlers to Guiana between 1763 and 1765, mostly Alsatians and Germans, to create a colony of European settlement. Poorly prepared, most died within a few months of fevers, dysentery and hunger; the survivors took refuge on islands off the coast, since known as the Salvation Islands, and many returned to France.

hechos/misiones-capuchinas-del-caroni/re.texto: Catalan Capuchins founded mission villages from 1724 between the Orinoco and the Caroní, with Caribs, Guayano and other peoples, which came to gather several thousand people and large herds of cattle. In 1817, during the patriot campaign in Guayana, the missions were seized to supply the army, and several captive Capuchins were killed at Caruachi by patriot soldiers, with responsibilities that historiography debates; the villages were depopulated.

hechos/revolucion-del-19-de-abril-de-181.texto: On news of the fall of almost all of Spain into French hands, the Caracas cabildo, enlarged with Creoles, forced the resignation of Captain General Vicente Emparan and formed a Supreme Junta that governed in the name of Ferdinand VII and disowned the Regency Council. The junta sent Bolívar, Andrés Bello and Luis López Méndez to London and called a congress.

hechos/revolucion-del-20-de-julio-de-181.texto: Amid the formation of provincial juntas (Cartagena, Cali, Pamplona, El Socorro), a quarrel between Creoles and the Spanish merchant José González Llorente over a vase (florero) was the occasion to convene an open cabildo that formed a governing junta. Viceroy Amar y Borbón presided over it for a few days and then was removed and expelled.

hechos/independencia-de-venezuela/titulo.texto: Independence of Venezuela and the First Republic

hechos/independencia-de-venezuela/resume.texto: The congress declared independence on July 5, 1811 and in December sanctioned a federal constitution. Coro, Maracaibo and Guayana remained loyal to the Regency and Valencia rebelled. After the earthquake of March 1812 and the advance of Domingo de Monteverde, Miranda capitulated at San Mateo in July 1812 and was handed over to the Spanish by patriot officers, among them Bolívar; the war continued until 1821.

hechos/terremoto-de-caracas-de-1812/resu.texto: On March 26, 1812, Holy Thursday, an earthquake destroyed much of Caracas, La Guaira, Barquisimeto, San Felipe and Mérida, with deaths estimated at between 15,000 and 20,000. Part of the clergy presented it as divine punishment for the rebellion; the phrase attributed to Bolívar about conquering nature comes from the account of the royalist José Domingo Díaz.

hechos/patria-boba/resumen.texto: The New Granada juntas failed to form a single government: the state of Cundinamarca, centralist and presided over by Nariño, and the federalist United Provinces of New Granada, with Camilo Torres, fought civil wars (1812-1814), while Santa Marta, Pasto and Popayán remained loyal to the king. The name “Patria Boba” (“Foolish Fatherland”), given by later historiography, is derogatory.

hechos/campana-admirable/titulo.texto: Admirable Campaign and War to the Death

hechos/campana-admirable/resumen.texto: Bolívar advanced from New Granada in May 1813 and entered Caracas in August, beginning the Second Republic. The war became one of reprisals against prisoners and civilians on both sides: in February 1814 Bolívar ordered some 800 Spanish and Canary Islander prisoners executed in La Guaira and Caracas, and royalist chiefs killed patriot prisoners and civilians.

hechos/guerra-de-1814/titulo.texto: Boves’s Offensive and the Fall of the Second Republic

hechos/guerra-de-1814/resumen.texto: Boves’s llaneros, mostly pardos, enslaved people and freedmen moved by promises of plunder and freedom, defeated Bolívar at La Puerta (June 1814) and took Valencia and Caracas, whose population fled en masse eastward. In Valencia, surrendered in July on the promise to spare lives, his troops killed many defenders and residents; Boves died in Urica in December. Laureano Vallenilla Lanz and Juan Uslar Pietri interpreted 1814 as a popular rebellion of pardos and enslaved people; Germán Carrera Damas questioned the image of Boves as a social reformer and stressed the weight of plunder.

hechos/sitio-de-cartagena-de-1815/resume.texto: Pablo Morillo’s expedition besieged Cartagena by land and sea from August until December 6, 1815; the city had declared absolute independence in 1811. Hunger and disease killed thousands of inhabitants; in February 1816 Morillo had nine leaders shot, remembered as the martyrs of Cartagena.

hechos/reconquista-de-nueva-granada/resu.texto: Morillo entered Santafé in May 1816 and set up a permanent war council and a sequestration board (junta de secuestros): dozens of patriot leaders were shot, among them Camilo Torres, Caldas and Jorge Tadeo Lozano, and others were exiled or lost their property. Colombian historiography calls those years the “régimen del terror” (“regime of terror”); the executions continued under Juan Sámano, such as that of Policarpa Salavarrieta in 1817.

hechos/congreso-de-angostura/resumen.texto: Congress of deputies from the Venezuelan provinces held by the patriots, joined by New Granadans, installed on February 15, 1819. It elected Bolívar president, sanctioned a constitution for Venezuela and on December 17 the Fundamental Law of the Republic of Colombia.

hechos/batalla-de-boyaca/resumen.texto: After crossing the Llanos and the páramo of Pisba with Venezuelan and New Granadan troops and British volunteers, the army of Bolívar and Santander defeated on August 7, 1819, by the bridge of Boyacá, the royalist division of José María Barreiro. Viceroy Sámano fled and Bolívar entered Santafé on August 10; in October Santander had Barreiro and other officer prisoners shot.

hechos/batalla-de-carabobo/resumen.texto: On June 24, 1821 Bolívar’s army, with Páez and the British Legion, defeated that of Miguel de la Torre on the Carabobo plain near Valencia. It decided the independence of Venezuela, although Puerto Cabello resisted until 1823.

hechos/congreso-de-cucuta/resumen.texto: Constituent congress meeting in the Villa del Rosario de Cúcuta between May and October 1821. It sanctioned the Constitution of the Republic of Colombia, elected Bolívar and Santander, approved the free-womb law (ley de libertad de vientres), suppressed the Inquisition and Indigenous tribute, and ordered the division of the resguardos.

hechos/gran-colombia/resumen.texto: State created at Angostura in 1819 that brought together Venezuela, New Granada, Panama (from 1821) and Quito (1822), and sustained the war in Peru. It was weakened by war debts, the rivalry between Caracas and Bogotá (La Cosiata, 1826), the conflict between Bolívar and Santander, Bolívar’s dictatorship (1828-1830) and the assassination attempt of September 1828. Venezuela and Ecuador separated in 1830, the year Bolívar died in Santa Marta.

hechos/toma-de-cartagena-por-drake/titul.texto: Capture of Cartagena by Francis Drake

hechos/toma-de-cartagena-por-drake/resum.texto: In February 1586 the English fleet of Francis Drake, at war with Spain, landed near Cartagena, took the city and occupied it for weeks, until the cabildo paid a ransom and Drake withdrew after setting fire to part of it. The attack led the Crown to fortify the port with plans by the engineer Bautista Antonelli.

hechos/saqueo-de-cartagena-de-1697/resum.texto: In April and May 1697, during the Nine Years’ War, a French squadron under the Baron de Pointis, with buccaneers and militia from Saint-Domingue led by Jean-Baptiste du Casse, took Cartagena and sacked it. Pointis carried off most of the loot, and the buccaneers, who felt cheated, sacked the city again.

hechos/la-vacuna-en-venezuela-y-nueva-gr.texto: Smallpox vaccination in Venezuela and New Granada

The expedition of Francisco Javier de Balmis reached Puerto Cabello in March 1804 with children carrying the vaccine, vaccinated people in Caracas and left there a junta in charge of preserving it; Andrés Bello dedicated an ode to it. From La Guaira, a branch under José Salvany continued through Cartagena, the Magdalena and Santafé (December 1804) toward Quito and Lima, vaccinating thousands of people along the way.

lugares/parque-arqueologico-de-san-agust.texto: Complex of burial mounds, tombs and hundreds of stone statues from the upper Magdalena, made mostly in the first millennium of the Common Era by societies whose name is unknown. Fray Juan de Santa Gertrudis described it in the mid-18th century, Konrad Theodor Preuss excavated it in 1913–1914, and it has been a World Heritage Site since 1995.

lugares/tierradentro/resumen.texto: Hypogea (underground tombs with a staircase, columns and walls painted with geometric motifs) carved into the rock of the Inzá hills, in Cauca, between roughly the 6th and 10th centuries. World Heritage Site since 1995; the region today belongs to the Nasa, who resisted the Spanish for a long time.

lugares/ciudad-perdida/resumen.texto: Tairona center in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta, with more than a hundred stone terraces linked by paths and stairways, founded around 800 AD and abandoned at the time of the conquest. Looters (guaqueros) found it in 1972, and the Colombian Institute of Anthropology has excavated it since 1976; the Kogi, Arhuaco and Wiwa consider it a sacred place.

lugares/laguna-de-guatavita/resumen.texto: Sacred lake of the Muisca northeast of Bogotá, associated with the ceremony of the gold-covered cacique that gave rise to the legend of El Dorado. Antonio de Sepúlveda dug a trench to drain it in 1580, and a British company partly emptied it at the beginning of the 20th century, with few finds; it has been protected since 1965.

lugares/templo-del-sol-de-sogamoso/nombr.texto: Temple of the Sun at Sogamoso

lugares/templo-del-sol-de-sogamoso/resum.texto: Muisca sanctuary of Sugamuxi, seat of the iraca, the religious leader. According to the chronicles, soldiers of Jiménez de Quesada who were looting it at night with torches set it on fire in September 1537. The Sogamoso Archaeological Museum has a modern reconstruction.

lugares/el-infiernito/resumen.texto: Archaeological site near Villa de Leyva with two alignments of stone columns and monoliths, from the Muisca period or earlier. That it functioned as an observatory for measuring the calendar is an interpretation by the archaeologists who studied it.

lugares/san-sebastian-de-uraba/resumen.texto: Fort that Alonso de Ojeda built in 1510 in the Gulf of Urabá. Surrounded by Indigenous people, who used poisoned arrows, and without food, the survivors under Francisco Pizarro abandoned it that same year.

lugares/santa-marta/resumen.texto: Founded by Rodrigo de Bastidas in 1525, it is the oldest Spanish city still inhabited in Colombia. It was the base for the wars against the Tairona and the starting point of Jiménez de Quesada’s expedition (1536); Bolívar died on its outskirts in 1830.

lugares/coro/resumen.texto: Founded in 1527 by Juan de Ampíes among the Caquetío people of the cacique Manaure, with whom he had made an agreement; it was the capital of the province of Venezuela during the Welser government. Site of the Chirino insurrection (1795); its historic center has been a World Heritage Site since 1993.

lugares/nueva-cadiz/resumen.texto: First town granted a city charter in Venezuelan territory, on the island of Cubagua, born from pearl fishing. The divers were Indigenous, many of them captured as slaves on the neighboring coasts and islands; Las Casas denounced the conditions. It was depopulated around 1541, once the pearl beds were exhausted.

lugares/cartagena-de-indias/resumen.texto: Founded in 1533 by Pedro de Heredia next to the Indigenous settlement of Calamarí. It was the main port of the New Granadan Caribbean, one of the ports authorized for the entry of enslaved Africans, seat of the Inquisition tribunal from 1610, and a fortified town; its walled precinct has been a World Heritage Site since 1984.

lugares/popayan/resumen.texto: Founded by Sebastián de Belalcázar in 1537; it depended on the Audiencia of Quito and was the center of a mining aristocracy that exploited gold from the Pacific coast with enslaved Africans. Birthplace of Camilo Torres and Caldas.

lugares/bogota/resumen.texto: Founded as Santafé on August 6, 1538 by Gonzalo Jiménez de Quesada, on lands of the Muisca zipa. It was the seat of the Royal Audiencia from 1550, of the archbishopric from 1564 and of the viceroyalty of New Granada from 1739; later, capital of Gran Colombia and of Colombia.

lugares/tunja/resumen.texto: Founded in 1539 by Gonzalo Suárez Rendón on Hunza, seat of the Muisca zaque. Capital of one of the most populous provinces of the New Kingdom, its visitas de indios (colonial inspections of Indigenous populations) are a central source for the history of the Muisca population.

lugares/caracas/resumen.texto: Founded by Diego de Losada in 1567, after the war with the valley’s caciques. It was the seat of the governorship of Venezuela from 1578 and later of the Captaincy General (1777), the Audiencia (1786) and the university (1721); there the junta of April 19, 1810 was formed.

lugares/cumana/resumen.texto: It emerged from the Franciscan missions set up on the coast around 1515 and from New Toledo, which Gonzalo de Ocampo founded in 1521; it is considered the oldest city still inhabited on the South American mainland coast. It was a base for pearl fishing and for the capture of Indigenous people to sell as slaves.

lugares/angostura/resumen.texto: Santo Tomé de Guayana moved in 1764 to the Angostura (narrows) of the Orinoco. From 1817 it was the capital of patriot Venezuela, and in 1819 the seat of the Congress of Angostura; today it is called Ciudad Bolívar.

lugares/paramaribo/resumen.texto: European trading post on the Suriname River from the early 17th century, capital of the English colony of Willoughby (1650) and, from 1667, of the Dutch colony of Suriname. Its historic center of wooden houses has been a World Heritage Site since 2002.

lugares/cayena/resumen.texto: French settlement from 1643, permanent from 1664 and capital of French Guiana. The Dutch took it in 1676, and a Portuguese-British force occupied it between 1809 and 1817.

lugares/san-basilio-de-palenque/resumen.texto: Town of descendants of runaway slaves (cimarrones) in the Montes de María, near Cartagena, which preserves the Palenquero language, a Creole with a Spanish base and Bantu contributions. UNESCO declared it a masterpiece of oral heritage in 2005. The date of its recognition by the Crown (1691 or 1713, depending on the author) and its relationship with Benkos Biohó are debated.

lugares/jodensavanne/resumen.texto: Settlement of Sephardic Jews on the banks of the Suriname River, with plantations worked by enslaved Africans and a synagogue from 1685 (Beracha ve Shalom). It declined in the 18th century and was abandoned after a fire in 1832.

lugares/fuerte-kyk-over-al/resumen.texto: Dutch fort on an island at the confluence of the Essequibo and the Mazaruni, seat of the Essequibo colony of the Dutch West India Company until the mid-18th century, and center of trade with the Caribs, who sold them Indigenous captives.

lugares/universidad-santo-tomas-bogota/n.texto: Universidad de Santo Tomás de Santafé

lugares/universidad-santo-tomas-bogota/r.texto: General study of the Dominicans in Santafé. A bull of Gregory XIII from 1580 authorized it, but degree-granting studies only began in the 17th century; it disappeared in the 19th century and was restored in 1965.

lugares/colegio-de-san-bartolome/resumen.texto: College founded by Archbishop Bartolomé Lobo Guerrero and entrusted to the Jesuits in 1604; the Academia Javeriana operated within it. After the expulsion of 1767 it passed to the secular clergy and trained many leaders of independence.

lugares/pontificia-universidad-javeriana.texto: Jesuit academy in Santafé authorized to award degrees in 1623. It closed with the expulsion of the Society of Jesus in 1767 and was restored in 1930.

lugares/colegio-del-rosario/nombre.texto: Colegio Mayor de Nuestra Señora del Rosario

lugares/colegio-del-rosario/resumen.texto: Founded in 1653 by the Dominican archbishop Cristóbal de Torres, with constitutions taken from the Colegio Mayor del Arzobispo of Salamanca. Mutis taught modern sciences there from 1762, and Camilo Torres and Caldas were trained in its classrooms.

lugares/universidad-central-de-venezuela.texto: Royal and Pontifical University of Caracas

Created by a Real Cédula of Philip V on December 22, 1721, over the seminary of Santa Rosa; it opened its courses in 1725. It was the first university in Venezuela; Bolívar gave it republican statutes in 1827.

lugares/hospital-san-juan-de-dios-bogota.texto: Hospital de San Juan de Dios de Santafé

It descends from the hospital that Fray Juan de los Barrios, the first archbishop of Santafé, founded in 1564; in the 17th century the Hospitaller Brothers of Saint John of God took it over, and its official founding under that name is dated 1723. It was Bogotá’s main hospital and medical school until it closed in 2001.

lugares/palacio-de-la-inquisicion-cartag.texto: Palace of the Inquisition in Cartagena

Seat of the Holy Office tribunal of Cartagena (1610–1821), with jurisdiction over the Caribbean and the New Kingdom; the present building was completed in 1770. The tribunal applied torture in some proceedings, as its rules allowed; some of the torture instruments displayed in its museum are replicas or reconstructions.

lugares/castillo-san-felipe-de-barajas/n.texto: Castillo de San Felipe de Barajas

lugares/castillo-san-felipe-de-barajas/r.texto: Fortress on the San Lázaro hill, begun in 1657 and expanded in the 18th century. In April 1741 its defenders repulsed the decisive British assault of Vernon’s expedition.

lugares/biblioteca-nacional-de-colombia/.texto: Opened in 1777 with books confiscated from the Jesuits, through the efforts of the fiscal (prosecutor) Moreno y Escandón; one of the first public libraries in America and the origin of the National Library of Colombia.

lugares/observatorio-astronomico-de-bogo.texto: Tower built in 1802–1803 at Mutis’s initiative as part of the Botanical Expedition; Caldas directed it until 1810. It is presented as the first observatory built in America, a title that depends on what is counted as one.

lugares/museo-del-oro/resumen.texto: Museum of the Banco de la República, created in 1939 with the purchase of a Quimbaya poporo; it holds the largest collection of pre-Hispanic goldwork in the world, including the Muisca raft.
